paragraph.text: J25. "A party with only vegan food excludes people who eat meat"

it's the other way round. People who eat meat also eat rice, beans, salad, pasta, fruit and sweets without animal ingredients; vegans don't eat meat. A vegan menu is the only one everyone present can eat, so it's the most inclusive. Nobody goes hungry because there's no meat, and nobody is forced into anything: the party simply doesn't offer one kind of food. Often the refusal doesn't even come from the food, but from the word "vegan": research shows that the label by itself lowers acceptance of dishes people would happily eat, and that there is prejudice against vegans. Refusing out of prejudice is disrespectful to people who chose a more ethical life, without animal exploitation. And it isn't the same as saying vegans disrespect people who eat meat: on one side there is an imposition on victims, the animals; on the other, there isn't.
"Making the school party vegan-only is an imposition. People who eat meat are left out."
At a party or group event, the menu should respect the preferences of the majority.
A vegan-only menu ignores that preference.
So a vegan-only menu excludes people who eat meat.

P1 is debatable: at a group event, the fairest criterion is that everyone can eat, not that the majority eats what they prefer. P2 is true. P3 is true, but ignoring a preference isn't excluding: people who eat meat can still eat everything that's served.

At a party with egg-free chocolate cake, popcorn and veggie hot dogs, everyone can eat. If there were only food with meat, some friends would have nothing to eat. The party where everyone can eat is the one that includes the most people. Sometimes someone won't even try the food just because they heard the word "vegan", and that isn't fair to whoever planned the party thinking of everyone and of the animals.

You can eat vegan food, but a vegan can't eat meat. That's why a vegan menu is the only one everyone can eat: it's the most inclusive, not the one that excludes. Nobody goes without food, nobody is banned from anything outside the event, and the party simply didn't offer one kind of dish. Is the rejection really of the food, or of the label? Research shows that the word "vegan" lowers the choice of dishes people would accept under another name. Refusing out of prejudice disrespects people who chose to live without exploiting animals. And that isn't equivalent to vegans "disrespecting" people who eat meat: only one side imposes something on victims, the animals.

text.bold: 1. Not having your favorite dish isn't exclusion.

paragraph.text: Excluding means stopping someone from taking part. People who eat meat take part and eat normally at a vegan party.

text.bold: 2. Vegan food is the most compatible.

paragraph.text: It also suits vegetarians, many people allergic to milk or eggs, and several religious restrictions, such as those of people who don't eat pork or beef.
Outside the party, everyone still eats what they want. The event just chose a menu, as it always does.

text.bold: 4. Many everyday dishes are already vegan.

paragraph.text: Rice, beans, salads, pasta with tomato sauce, fruit, popcorn and many sweets have no animal ingredients.

text.bold: 5. Often the refusal is of the label, not the food.

paragraph.text: People who say they'll go hungry at a vegan party often eat, on other days, the same dishes without noticing they're vegan. Research suggests the problem is often the word. In an experiment with more than 7,000 US adults, published in 2024, a basket of food without meat or dairy was chosen by 20% of participants when called "vegan" and by more than 40% when called "healthy" or "sustainable". Another study, from 2017, found prejudice against vegetarians and vegans: people who eat meat rated them as negatively as, or more negatively than, several groups commonly targeted by prejudice, and rated vegans more negatively than vegetarians. These studies come from Western countries and don't measure any particular party, but they show that rejection can come from an idea about vegans, not from the taste. Refusing a dish out of prejudice is disrespectful to whoever made it and to people who chose a more ethical life, without animal exploitation.

text.bold: 6. "But vegans disrespect meat eaters too" is a false equivalence.

paragraph.text: The usual reply is that vegans disrespect non-vegans when they turn down meat or criticize eating it. But the two situations aren't the same. Someone who eats meat suffers no harm at a vegan party: they eat normally, and nothing is taken from them outside it. Eating meat, on the other hand, involves an imposition on victims, the animals, who are bred and killed without being able to refuse. Disagreeing with a practice that harms others isn't the same as looking down on someone for not causing that harm. Treating the two as equal is a false equivalence, and answering a criticism with "you too" is the
. None of this entitles either side to treat the other with contempt; it only shows that the two complaints don't weigh the same.
